claims.text: Nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors synchronizes their co-nucleation.
Synchronized co-nucleation drives homogeneous atomic mixing and formation of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Temporal separation of precursor reduction events permits phase-segregated nucleation.
The initial material is a uniformly mixed blend of noble-metal salts or complexes corresponding to the desired alloy elements.
Controlling the temperature ramp rate through the reduction regime can force the reduction kinetics of all metals into a narrow time window.
The comparison holds precursor concentrations and support conditions constant.
Processing is conducted under an inert or reducing atmosphere.
The control ramp rate is previously known to produce some phase separation.
Early nucleation of one element creates segregated domains.
Narrowing the precursor-reduction interval overcomes differences among the individual metals' reduction energies.
Simultaneous reduction and nucleation promote co-nucleation rather than formation of spatially separated phases.
A tuned ramp rate will produce a more homogeneous atomic-scale elemental distribution than the control ramp rate.
A broader control ramp permits staggered reduction events.
Staggered reduction events typically result in elemental segregation or phase separation.

The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles processed under inert or reducing atmospheres without additional ligands or capping agents that independently alter nucleation kinetics.
The mechanism should not be generalized to systems whose kinetics are dominated by factors unrelated to reduction synchronization.
The precise quantitative reduction in phase separation cannot be predicted without systematic kinetic studies.
Failure of the tuned-ramp sample to show a statistically significant improvement in elemental homogeneity over the control would falsify the proposed governing role of synchronized reduction.
